claim: Sandi Metz, The Wrong Abstraction (2016-01-20): duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction; remedy is to re-introduce duplication by inlining
quotes: duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction
Re-introduce duplication by inlining the abstracted code back into every caller.
Within each caller, use the parameters being passed to determine the subset of the inlined code that this specific caller executes.
Delete the bits that aren't needed for this particular caller.
When dealing with the wrong abstraction, the fastest way forward is back .
Posted on January 20, 2016 by Sandi Metz
note: The post says it was originally written for her Chainline Newsletter; the phrase itself was circulating on Twitter by March 2014 (embedded tweet dated March 7, 2014), so 2016-01-20 is the blog republication date, not the first use of the phrase.

claim: Rule of three, attributed to Don Roberts in Fowler's Refactoring (1999; 2nd ed 2018)
quotes: Rule of three ( "Three strikes and you refactor" ) is a code refactoring rule of thumb
The rule was popularised by Martin Fowler in Refactoring [ 1 ] and attributed to Don Roberts.
(c2 wiki quoting Refactoring 1st ed. p58) The first time you do something, you just do it.
The second time you do something similar, you wince at the duplication, but you do the duplicate thing anyway.
The third time you do something similar, you refactor.
source_date: Wikipedia fetched 2026-10-04 (cites Fowler, Beck, Brant, Opdyke, Roberts 1999, Addison-Wesley, ISBN 978-0201485677); c2 page dated November 22, 2014
note: Book text not reachable online from a primary source; both citations are secondary (Wikipedia cites the 1999 book; c2 quotes 1st ed. p58). 'Three strikes and you refactor' is confirmed only as Wikipedia's parenthetical name and the c2 page title, not verified as a verbatim book line. 2nd edition (2018) wording not checked.

claim: Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design: 2nd ed 2021; deep modules, classitis, information leakage, pull complexity downwards, define errors out of existence, complexity definition
quotes: In July of 2021 I released the Second Edition of A Philosophy of Software Design .
Deep class: small interface, lots of functionality
Classitis: small classes taken to the extreme
Information leakage: opposite of information hiding
Pull complexity down into modules: Let a few module developers suffer, rather than thousands of users
Whenever possible, define errors out of existence

claim: PEP 387 deprecation rule; PEP 565 DeprecationWarning shown by default only in __main__; FutureWarning is for end users
quotes: Wait for the warning to appear in at least two minor Python versions of the same major version, or one minor version in an older major version
It is preferred, though, to wait 5 years before removal (e.g., warn starting in Python 3.10, removal in 3.15
(PEP 565) DeprecationWarning: reported by default for code that runs directly in the __main__ module ... but hidden by default for code in other modules.
(PEP 565) FutureWarning: reported by default for all code. The intended audience is users of applications written in Python
(warnings docs) FutureWarning Base class for warnings about deprecated features when those warnings are intended for end users of applications that are written in Python.
source_date: PEP 387 Active, created 18-Jun-2009, last discussed 16-Jun-2023; PEP 565 Final, Python 3.7, created 12-Nov-2017; Python 3 docs fetched 2026-10-04
note: Rule is 'at least two minor versions' (warn in 3.N, remove no earlier than 3.N+2), with 5 years preferred.

claim: McCabe 1976 (IEEE TSE) cyclomatic complexity, suggested limit 10; radon CC rank table and MI formula
quotes: (McCabe 1976) The particular upper bound that has been used for cyclomatic complexity is 10 which seems like a reasonable, but not magical, upper limit.
When the complexity exceeded 10 they had to either recognize and modularize subfunctions or redo the software.
(radon) CC score Rank Risk 1 - 5 A low - simple block 6 - 10 B low - well structured and stable block 11 - 20 C moderate - slightly complex block 21 - 30 D more than moderate
31 - 40 E high - complex block, alarming 41+ F very high - error-prone, unstable block
(radon) Radon uses another derivative, computed from both SEI derivative and Visual Studio one: MI = max[0, 100 (171 - 5.2 ln V - 0.23 G - 16.2 ln L + 50 sin(sqrt(2.4 C))) / 171]
(radon) MI score Rank Maintainability 100 - 20 A Very high 19 - 10 B Medium 9 - 0 C Extremely low
source_date: T. J. McCabe, 'A Complexity Measure', IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, Vol. SE-2, No. 4, December 1976, p. 308 ff; radon docs latest (radon 6.0.1, 2023)
note: McCabe PDF is a scanned copy hosted on literateprogramming.com (third-party host of the original paper); text via pdftotext, spaces normalised. In the MI formula V = Halstead Volume, G = total cyclomatic complexity, L = SLOC, C = percent comment lines converted to radians. Radon MI ranks are A/B/C only (not A-F).
